title: Chart: A record two-thirds of car sales in China are now electric vehicles
text:
Using China Passenger Car Association data, Carbon Brief shows that new-energy vehicles reached 67% of new car sales in September 2026, indicating that electrification is shifting from subsidy-led expansion toward self-reinforcing market growth and now affects global auto trade and oil demand through exports and transport substitution.

The shift comes after the Hormuz crisis raised fuel costs, suggesting that external energy shocks are accelerating transport electrification rather than merely causing temporary disruption. The September 2026 sales data provide the latest window into a structural turn in China’s auto market.

This sits at the intersection of China’s transport electrification agenda, changing oil demand, and export competition in the auto industry.

title: Experts: How are climate scientists using artificial intelligence?
text:
By assembling expert views, Carbon Brief shows that AI is now being used in weather prediction, satellite-image analysis and climate-policy support, but its energy demand, weak verifiability and tendency to widen scientific inequalities imply that research institutions need validation standards, energy constraints and equitable access rules at the same time.

The AI boom is rapidly entering climate-science workflows; without method checks and allocation rules, gains in performance may come with new bias and inequality. The piece responds to this governance gap at the moment of expansion.

This sits at the intersection of climate-science methods, research governance and policy-tool deployment.

title: Climate may have slipped down the Annual Meetings agenda, but remains on the balance sheet
text:
E3G argues that climate may have receded from the main stage at the Bangkok IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, but energy insecurity, extreme weather and fiscal pressure still keep climate risk on governments’ balance sheets, so multilateral development banks and finance tools must embed preventive adaptation investment and rapid post-shock support in routine financial arrangements.

The piece uses the Annual Meetings window to show climate being recoded by fiscal and risk-management logic rather than just by agenda rhetoric. It responds directly to current constraints on sovereign finance and adaptation investment.

This sits at the intersection of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, development finance and the mainstreaming of climate risk.

title: EU ETS – Foundation for a Green Steel Ecosystem
text:
E3G argues that the EU Emissions Trading System can support green steel only if it is paired with complementary legislation, demand-side signals and industrial policy; otherwise pioneering projects will not become financeable, replicable low-carbon capacity and the transition will remain fragmented.

Europe is moving heavy-industry decarbonization from pilots to system-building, making the adequacy of the carbon-price, regulatory and market-building mix a live issue. The piece recasts the ETS as institutional foundation rather than a stand-alone abatement tool.

This sits at the intersection of EU industrial decarbonization, carbon-market design and competitiveness policy.

title: Multilateral Climate Finance in Pursuit of Private Capital: How the De-Risking Agenda Is Changing International Organizations
source: Erin R. Graham, Jiayi (Sonia) Zhang · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article argues that multilateral climate finance is being reshaped by a de-risking agenda: international organizations increasingly use multilateral funds to mobilize institutional investors and domestic banks rather than finance individual mitigation or adaptation projects, blurring the line between economic and environmental IOs and creating transparency problems.

The authors combine text analysis of replenishment documents from five climate-finance international organizations with an assessment of GEF and GCF projects to compare how de-risking changes funding use and organizational roles.

Read alongside E3G’s "Climate may have slipped down the Annual Meetings agenda, but remains on the balance sheet" to see how adaptation and risk finance are being rewritten into multilateral financial rules.

Who benefits from de-risking in multilateral climate finance? multilateral climate finance de-risking institutional investors transparency How does de-risking reshape climate-finance allocation? GCF GEF financial intermediation climate projects

title: Theorizing Access in Global Environmental Governance: A Critical Analysis of COP26 and the COVID-19 Pandemic
source: Lauren M. Baker, Diana K. Elhard, Kimberly R. Marion Suiseeya, Laura Zanotti, Margaret O’Connell, Alexandra Anderson · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article argues that access in global environmental governance cannot be reduced to attendance or open registration; collaborative event ethnography at COP26 shows that discriminatory design, technological disparities and recognitional injustice obstruct sustained, meaningful participation and deepen power asymmetries.

The authors use collaborative event ethnography at COP26 and draw on critical disability studies to rethink the differences among access, accessibility and inclusion.

Read with this issue’s COP17 biodiversity process stories and Inside Climate News’s "Battleground Ballots" to see how accessibility and political mobilization jointly shape governance outcomes.

How does conference accessibility affect negotiation outcomes? global environmental governance accessibility COP participation How do technological barriers amplify inequality in climate diplomacy? digital inequality inclusion conference participation disability studies

title: COP17: Which countries have released new pledges to tackle nature loss?
text:
Carbon Brief shows that 113 parties have now submitted updated NBSAPs, yet the Kunming-Montreal 2030 targets remain well off track; the central issue is not whether pledges exist, but whether they enter a comparable, trackable, and reviewable global process linked to finance, monitoring, and national reporting.

This analysis lands on the COP17 global review window, when countries will be assessed on updated commitments toward the 2030 targets. The original deadline has already been widely missed, so the gap between submission and implementation is now the negotiation’s core problem.

Direct input into the COP17 global review and the implementation agenda under the Kunming-Montreal framework.

title: COP17: Tracking progress towards the UN’s 2030 nature targets
text:
By tracking all 23 targets one by one, Carbon Brief argues that the bottleneck in nature governance has shifted from having a framework to knowing which targets are actually advancing, and the fact that 22 targets are off track shows that finance, subsidy reform, restoration, and monitoring still lack institutional coherence; the piece effectively argues for putting budgets, accountability, and implementation timing on the same ledger.

Published just before COP17, it provides the first global map of where progress is lagging by target. It challenges broad-brush claims and forces negotiators to confront the distribution of implementation failures.

Technical background for the COP17 progress review and the text negotiations that follow.

title: Explained: Reforms to the IMF and World Bank’s debt framework send a new climate signal – adaptation counts
text:
E3G argues that after the IMF and World Bank revised the Low-Income Countries Debt Sustainability Framework, debt assessments now take climate vulnerability and adaptation investment more seriously, meaning multilateral financial rules are beginning to treat adaptation not as an extra cost but as part of debt realism and development resilience.

This explainer responds to policy changes around the 2026 annual meetings, showing that the debt framework is no longer a purely fiscal tool but now absorbs climate risk. It offers an institutional entry point for adaptation finance.

Policy interpretation of the revised MDB and IMF debt framework, part of the post-annual-meetings implementation agenda.

title: The BRICS Sustainability Paradox in Global Governance
source: Hendry Roris P. Sianturi, Uud Wahyudin, Budi Nugraha, Reddy Anggara · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The authors argue that ‘green growth’ and ‘responsible tourism’ in the BRICS often function as legitimacy performance rather than structural transformation; the communication–implementation gap shows that sustainability language can mask continuity unless independent verification, impact-based metrics, and Southern epistemologies are brought in.

This is a Global Forum-style conceptual analysis that uses tourism as the lens for examining the sustainability gap in governance.

Read alongside this week’s Carbon Brief coverage of COP17 pledges and UN News reporting from Armenia, since both ask how commitments become verifiable implementation.

How do Southern epistemologies alter verification of sustainability pledges? Southern epistemologies verification global governance sustainability metrics Why does tourism magnify the implementation gap in sustainability governance? tourism governance implementation gap legitimacy global governance

title: Democratization, International Knowledge Institutions, and Global Governance
text:
The author argues that international knowledge institutions constrain power in global governance by setting standards for reasoning and deliberation, classifying objects of international discourse, and shaping participation; knowledge production itself therefore requires democratic critique.

This is a theory-driven article offering normative and conceptual analysis of the functions of international knowledge institutions.

Read alongside this issue’s two Carbon Brief COP17 pieces, since both deal with how targets, indicators, and reporting shape governance power.

How do indicators shape power in global environmental governance? indicators knowledge institutions global governance accountability Who gets to define compliance standards in international regimes? compliance standards participation international institutions

title: Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP17 biodiversity summit
text:
Carbon Brief’s tracker maps the COP17 and protocol texts and shows the Kunming-Montreal framework entering its midpoint check while 22 of 23 targets are off track; the real contest is over legal wording, committee jurisdiction, the division of labor across SBSTTA/SBI/SB8J, and parallel progress on the Cartagena and Nagoya Protocols, meaning the bottleneck is enforceable text and institutional coordination rather than slogans.

The Yerevan talks are about to begin, and this tracker turns a dispersed agenda into the text battles that will matter over the next two weeks. The midpoint review means parties must convert targets into negotiable, accountable draft decisions.

This is a preparatory tool for CBD COP17 and the two protocols, directly serving the Yerevan negotiating session.

title: Towards AZEC 2.0: Trends in the Philippines
titleOriginal: AZEC 2.0に向けて：フィリピンの動向
text:
E3G argues that if AZEC 2.0 remains centered on fuel supply security, support for the Philippine power sector may lock into fossil-fuel fixes and short-term patching; a more useful package would align Japanese technology, the Philippines’ drive to reduce imported fuel dependence, and actual power-sector decarbonization through grid upgrades, storage, renewables expansion and financing design.

Japan has launched AZEC 2.0 and POWERR Asia after the recent energy shock, and this analysis tests whether the new frame will translate into clean-power projects in the Philippines rather than fuel lock-in. As this year’s host country, the Philippines gives the project mix added signaling power.

This is a policy-steering note ahead of the 2026 AZEC summit and ministerial meeting, and an advocacy effort to shape project and finance priorities under the regional resilience narrative.

title: 2030 and beyond: Benchmarks for the energy transition and clean electrification
text:
Anchored in the COP31 Presidents’ 35-by-35 target, E3G argues that reaching 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035 can deliver both economic and energy-security gains; the policy lesson is that countries must link electrification, clean supply, system investment and industrial policy into a single 2030s pathway rather than treating the transition as isolated generation expansion.

This benchmark frame responds to the COP31 process around the 2035 electrification goal and provides a reference point for investment and policy in the 2030s. The key now is not only setting targets, but defining what counts as a 1.5°C-aligned pathway.

This is a policy-benchmark paper tied to the COP31 Presidency’s ‘35-by-35’ agenda.

title: Factcheck: UK Conservatives double the ‘cost of net-zero’ after spreadsheet blunder
text:
Carbon Brief shows the UK Conservatives overstated the cost of net zero in a booklet, and the issue is not only arithmetic error but the use of cost narratives as a political mobilization tool to reshape the acceptability of climate policy; the dispute increasingly turns on accounting conventions, communications strategy and policy credibility rather than real system-cost comparison.

The factcheck responds directly to the UK campaign narrative around net-zero costs, especially as fiscal and cost-of-living pressures remain elevated. It also offers an immediate case for how parties frame climate policy as a burden.

This is campaign material in UK climate and energy politics, not tied to a single negotiating venue.

title: Who Shapes Air Pollution Governance? How Economic Development, Democracy, and Data Condition Stakeholder Influence in Six Majority World Cities
source: Ella Henninger, E. Keith Smith, Thomas Bernauer · Global Environmental Politics
text:
Using six highly polluted majority-world cities, 63 semi-structured interviews, and 72 experts and stakeholders, the article compares how economic development, democracy, and data availability shape the influence of citizens, local advocates, economic elites, and country-external agencies over governments’ air-pollution efforts. It finds that governments remain primarily responsive to economic elites across development levels; external actors matter more in the poorest case, Dhaka; democracy strengthens citizens and advocates through electoral accountability and civil society mobilization; and data availability both opens influence opportunities and triggers government counterstrategies.

The authors combine semi-structured interviews across six Majority World cities with comparative analysis of stakeholder influence under differing institutional conditions.

Read alongside this issue’s 'How a Bid to Beat Drought Drove Corpus Christi to the Brink of Disaster,' which similarly exposes tensions between technical fixes, public accountability and governance capacity.

How does data availability reshape accountability in air pollution governance? air pollution governance data availability stakeholder influence accountability Does democracy amplify local advocacy in environmental governance? democracy civil society mobilization urban pollution political accountability

title: How Information About Disaster Vulnerability Shapes Climate Policy Preferences
source: Talbot M. Andrews, Richard Clark, Rebecca Perlman · Global Environmental Politics
text:
Using original survey experiments in the United States, the article examines how information about disaster vulnerability shifts public priorities between adaptation and mitigation. It finds that weak-prior respondents told about their exposure to extreme weather prioritize local adaptation over mitigation, while strong-prior respondents remain largely unmoved. The effects are especially consistent among independents, suggesting that mobilizing support for mitigation is harder when adaptation and mitigation compete for scarce budgets.

The authors run original survey experiments in the United States to estimate how vulnerability information causally affects policy preferences across prior attitudes.

Read alongside this issue’s Corpus Christi desalination story, as both show how adaptation projects run into fiscal constraints, risk perceptions and political support limits.

Does risk information increase support for adaptation? risk communication adaptation preference survey experiment climate policy How does budget competition reshape support for mitigation? budget constraint adaptation vs mitigation policy tradeoff public opinion

title: Analysis: Wind and solar save UK from gas imports worth £5.9bn during Hormuz crisis
text:
Record wind and solar output allowed the UK to avoid roughly £5.9bn in gas imports during the Hormuz crisis, showing that power-sector decarbonization has become a macro-stabilizer under external shocks; policy should treat transmission, storage, and demand-side flexibility as core energy-security infrastructure.

The analysis responds directly to the Middle East conflict-driven price spike and offers a quantified counterfactual: without renewable build-out, the UK would face a much larger import bill and a more fragile supply chain. It also shifts the meaning of energy security from fossil-fuel supply to system flexibility.

This is an immediate intervention in UK energy-security and power-market design debates, with implications for winter supply planning and storage investment priorities.

title: From energy shock to economic stability: Three tests for the Bangkok Annual Meetings
text:
E3G argues that the Bangkok World Bank and IMF Annual Meetings should treat energy shocks as macro-financial problems, using multilateral development banks, risk-sharing instruments, and debt arrangements to shield Asian economies; otherwise high rates and financing scarcity will crowd the transition out of the development agenda.

The argument speaks directly to the World Bank and IMF Annual Meetings in mid-October, making this a timely window to re-link energy-price volatility with development finance. It seeks to reopen policy space between fiscal tightening and transition investment.

This is a pre-meetings agenda-setting piece aimed at shaping how finance ministers, central bankers, and development institutions frame the financing architecture.

title: Europe’s clean industrial strategy needs a comprehensive lead-market architecture
text:
E3G argues that the EU must align the revised Public Procurement Act with the Industrial Accelerator Act to create stable demand for low-carbon materials and products; otherwise planned investment will not become European industrial capacity. The key is turning demand-side rules into a predictable market architecture.

The piece lands right after the Commission’s procurement-rule revision proposal, showing that Europe’s clean industrial policy has moved from slogan to institutional assembly. The current contest is over who creates demand, not whether transition is desirable.

This is a companion agenda item in the EU clean-industrial and procurement reform process, directly affecting how industrial competitiveness and decarbonization demand are institutionalized.

title: Public Opinion and the Political Logic of International Climate Pledges
source: Michaël Aklin, Mark T. Buntaine, Matto Mildenberger · Global Environmental Politics
text:
Using experiments across ten high-emitting countries and more than 10,000 respondents, the article shows that post-Paris public climate pledges are not only external signals but also domestic information about policy intent and bargaining posture. Publics generally prefer ambitious unilateral pledges, but at high ambition levels they favor conditional pledges that emphasize fairness. Counterpart conditional pledges do not automatically raise support for domestic action, and they increase support for transfers to low- and middle-income countries only when paired with ambitious unconditional pledges.

The authors ran three experiments across ten high-emitting countries with more than 10,000 respondents to test how different pledge types shape public preferences.

This issue’s “A Supreme Court Battle Over Climate Change Begins” shows domestic responsibility allocation moving from pledge politics into litigation, making it a useful counterpart to this article’s account of how publics read climate commitments.

When do conditional pledges become more persuasive domestically? climate pledges public opinion conditional commitments experiments How do pledges shape support for international climate transfers? international transfers climate finance pledge politics public opinion

title: Beyond Membership
source: Elise Doumergue, Hussam Hussein · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The article explains why states pursue observer status in regional international organizations despite lacking voting rights: it can signal recognition and cooperation intent, provide access to social networks for information and influence, and enhance prestige through collective recognition. Using twenty-one practitioner interviews, official documents, and diplomatic communications, the authors show that observer status is an underexamined but strategically useful diplomatic tool with practical, relational, and symbolic value.

The authors analyze original empirical material combining twenty-one practitioner interviews, official documents, and diplomatic communications.

This issue’s “The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all | Editorial” reminds us that domestic politics outside regional and global bodies can reshape cooperation incentives, a useful complement to this article’s discussion of observer status as diplomacy.

When does observer status increase influence? observer status regional organizations diplomacy international institutions How does non-member participation shape governance order? non-member participation institutional design regional governance status signaling

title: Analysis: Lula presidency saved at least 20,000km2 of Brazilian Amazon since 2022
text:
Carbon Brief’s analysis argues that Lula’s government, by re-enforcing the forest code, restoring environmental enforcement, and constraining illegal logging networks, has prevented at least 20,000 square kilometres of Amazon loss. It shows that forest governance in Brazil is not about abstract pledges but about the institutional struggle among federal enforcement, agribusiness interests, and electoral competition, implying the need to link regulation, budget authority, and constraints on local illegal economies.

The finding lands in the run-up to a new Brazilian election, when Lula and the Bolsonaro camp are closely matched and Amazon policy could swing sharply. It also pulls the slogan of “Brazil is back” back onto the terrain of domestic enforceable institutions.

This sits at the intersection of the Brazilian presidential race, forest-code enforcement, and COP climate commitments.

title: ‘Concerning’ low sea ice persists as Antarctic hits third-lowest winter peak
text:
Using NSIDC data, Carbon Brief argues that Antarctic sea ice has stayed at unusually low levels for several years, raising the question not of one seasonal minimum but of a possible structural downward shift. That makes tighter links among polar observation, attribution research, and climate risk assessment necessary, because sea-ice change feeds back into ocean circulation, weather anomalies, and risk-warning frameworks in governance.

The piece follows the latest satellite release and stresses that the immediate task is not explaining one low reading but judging whether a new state has been reached. By juxtaposing Antarctic and Arctic ice, it also signals a shifting polar-risk narrative.

This sits at the intersection of polar observing systems, attribution research, and climate-risk governance.

title: Climate Governance Antagonisms: Policy Stability and Repoliticization
source: Matthew Paterson, Paul Tobin, Stacy D. VanDeveer · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The authors set two common climate-governance strategies against each other: one prioritizes policy stability, institutional lock-in, and irreversibility; the other sees conflict and repoliticization as necessary to weaken incumbent power blocking ambitious mitigation. The article’s main contribution is not to endorse one path but to call for research on how stability and conflict interact in opening political space for rapid transformation.

The article uses a forum-style conceptual argument and research agenda setting, drawing on a synthetic discussion of climate politics literature.

Read with this issue’s Carbon Brief piece on Brazilian Amazon governance: does forest protection depend on institutional stability, or on electoral conflict that repoliticizes enforcement?

When do stability and conflict become complementary in climate politics? climate governance policy stability political conflict institutional change How does repoliticization open space for decarbonization? repoliticization decarbonization incumbent power political opportunity

title: Resilience, Adaptability and Transformability in Social-ecological Systems
source: Brian Walker, C. S. Holling, Stephen R. Carpenter and Ann Kinzig · Ecology and Society
text:
Walker and colleagues distinguish resilience, adaptability, and transformability to ask whether a social-ecological system should preserve existing functions, adjust its pathway, or deliberately transform when the old structure becomes untenable. The article links ecological feedbacks, institutional learning, cross-scale interaction, and actor capacity in one framework. Its key insight is that stability is not always desirable: some stable states lock in vulnerability and inequality. This helps interpret adaptation, biodiversity, and food-system policies by asking what should be maintained, what should change, and when transformation is necessary.

The article uses social-ecological systems theory and conceptual modeling. It identifies system mechanisms, but concrete policy application requires additional case evidence.

Read with this issue’s Carbon Brief report on persistently low Antarctic sea ice: is the polar system still in a stable regime, or has it crossed a threshold that demands transformation?

When should governance abandon a stable regime? resilience thresholds adaptability transformability How do polar changes trigger transformation governance? polar climate sea ice social-ecological systems governance
